newsitem.title: DUBAI: 238 sign up to run in Iran presidential election.
newsitem.headline: 238 sign up to run in Iran presidential election.

text.p: Iran said on Monday 238 people had signed up to run in next month's presidential election to replace President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.

Interior Minister Ali Mohammad Besharati, quoted by Tehran radio, said the list of the 238 had been handed over to the Guardian Council, a body of lawyers and Shi'ite Moslem clerics which will screen them in the next 10 days.
The powerful council disqualified all but a handful of those who signed up to run in past polls. In the last election in 1993 in approved four out of 128.

A dozen prominent figures have announced their intention to run in the May 23 election. Candidates will be screened for their allegience to Iran's religious leadership and the Islamic system of government established after the 1979 revolution.
Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei has banned newspapers receiving state funds from providing publicity for a particular candidate, Tehran newspapers said on Monday.

A statement by Khamenei's office asked a body overseeing election publicity to remind all such publications that "they absolutely do not have the right to act as the organ of a particular wing or tendency", the newspapers said.

The move came after the daily Hamshahri, published by the Tehran municipality, was accused by backers of the conservative candidate, Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, of mostly covering his main rival Mohammad Khatami.
Tehran's mayor is a leading figure among pro-Rafsanjani centrists who have backed Khatami, a former minister of culture and Islamic guidance.
The elections appeared to be shaping up as a two-horse race between Nateq-Nouri and Khatami. Former intelligence minister Mohammad Mohammadi Reyshahri is rated as another strong entrant.

Khamenei's statement named Hamshahri, the newspaper Iran which is published by the official news agency IRNA, and the dailies Kayhan and Ettelaat as publications that get state funds and should provide equal coverage to all candidates.
It said the rule applied to all publications receiving any public funds but did not say if that included those printed on subsidised newsprint -- which would cover most newspapers.
The daily Resalat, close to conservative clerics and bazaar merchants, has openly backed Nateq-Nouri while the newspaper Salam, published by radical Islamist intellectuals, has sided with Khatami.
Khatami's backers have accused the state television and radio of giving wide coverage to events involving Nateq-Nouri in his official capacity and ignoring their candidate.
Rafsanjani is barred by the constitution from running for a third consecutive four-year term. His term ends on August 3.
Official campaigning will be allowed for 12 days, up to the day before the vote, after the list of approved candidates is announced by the Guardian Council.
